risks.risk_description: Challenges in understanding or explaining the decision-making processes of AI systems, which can lead to mistrust, difficulty in enforcing compliance standards or holding relevant actors accountable for harms, and the inability to identify and correct errors.

mitigations.action_name: Red team third-party models before adoption
mitigations.description: Apply comprehensive AI red teaming and evaluations when selecting a third-party model. Use benchmarks such as Decoding Trust and conduct extensive use-case-specific red teaming beyond standard benchmarks.
Establish policies and procedures that address GAI data redundancy, including model weights and other system artifacts.

mitigations.action_name: Use centralized ML model registry
mitigations.description: Use a centralized ML model inventory and registry for models in production, ensuring proper governance, access control, and tracking of all deployed model versions.

mitigations.action_name: Implement automated MLOps deployment governance
mitigations.description: Implement automated MLOps deployment with governance, tracking, and approval workflows to tighten access and deployment controls for production model management.
Review various transparency artifacts (e.g., system cards and model cards) for third-party models.

Apply explainable AI (XAI) techniques (e.g., analysis of embeddings, model compression/distillation, gradient-based attributions, occlusion/term reduction, counterfactual prompts, word clouds) as part of ongoing continuous improvement processes to mitigate risks related to unexplainable GAI systems.

Document how pre-trained models have been adapted (e.g., fine-tuned, or retrieval-augmented generation) for the specific generative task, including any data augmentations, parameter adjustments, or other modifications. Access to un-tuned (baseline) models support s debugging the relative influence of the pre-trained weights compared to the fine-tuned model weights or other system updates.
Document the extent to which human domain knowledge is employed to improve GAI system performance, via, e.g., RLHF, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, content moderation, business rules.
Apply and document ML explanation results such as: Analysis of embeddings, Counterfactual prompts, Gradient-based attributions, Model compression/surrogate models, Occlusion/term reduction.

Document GAI model details including: Proposed use and organizational value; Assumptions and limitations, Data collection methodologies; Data provenance; Data quality; Model architecture (e.g., convolutional neural network, transformers, etc.); Optimization objectives; Training algorithms; RLHF approaches; Fine-tuning or retrieval-augmented generation approaches; Evaluation data; Ethical considerations; Legal and regulatory requirements.
Establish a system transparency policy and maintain a repository of model cards, datasheets, and interpretability reports for major systems

mitigations.action_name: Communicate misinformation risks to users
mitigations.description: Identify and communicate risks and possible harms of LLM-generated content, including the potential for misinformation, to all users and stakeholders.

mitigations.action_name: Design APIs and UIs for responsible LLM use
mitigations.description: Design APIs and user interfaces that encourage responsible use of LLM outputs. Integrate content filters, clearly label AI-generated content, inform users about reliability limitations, and specify intended field-of-use constraints.

Establish organizational roles, policies, and procedures for communicating GAI incidents and performance to AI Actors and downstream stakeholders ( including those potentially impacted), via community or official resources (e.g., AI incident database, AVID, CVE, NVD, or OECD AI incident monitor).

Create mechanisms to p rovide protections for whistleblowers who report, based on reasonable belief, when the organization violates relevant laws or poses a specific and empirically well-substantiated negative risk to public safety (or has already caused harm) .

Establish organizational practices to identify the minimum set of criteria necessary for GAI system incident reporting such as: System ID (auto-generated most likely), Title, Reporter, System/Source, Data Reported, Date of Incident, Description, Impact(s), Stakeholder(s) Impacted.
Verify information sharing and feedback mechanisms among individuals and organizations regarding any negative impact from GAI systems.
Document interactions with GAI systems to users prior to interactive activities, particularly in contexts involving more significant risks.
Document incidents involving third-party GAI data and systems, including open-data and open-source software.
Establish and maintain policies and procedures to record and track GAI system reported errors, near-misses, and negative impacts.

Consider disclosing use of GAI to end users in relevant contexts, while considering the objective of disclosure, the context of use, the likelihood and magnitude of the risk posed, the audience of the disclosure, as well as the frequency of the disclosures.
Share results of pre-deployment testing with relevant GAI Actors, such as those with system release approval authority.

Compile statistics on actual policy violations, take-down requests, and intellectual property infringement for organizational GAI systems: Analyze transparency reports across demographic groups, languages groups .
Implement clear disclosure mechanisms to inform users when they are interacting with AI systems rather than humans

Establish policies and procedures that address continual improvement processes for GAI risk measurement. Address general risks associated with a lack of explainability and transparency in GAI systems by using ample documentation and techniques such as: application of gradient-based attributions, occlusion/term reduction, counterfactual prompts and prompt engineering, and analysis of embeddings; Assess and update risk measurement approaches at regular cadences.
Use visualizations or other methods to represent GAI model behavior to ease non-technical stakeholders understanding of GAI system functionality.
Implement interpretability and explainability methods to evaluate GAI system decisions and verify alignment with intended purpose.

Assess the accuracy, quality, reliability, and authenticity of GAI output by comparing it to a set of known ground truth data and by using a variety of evaluation methods (e.g., human oversight and automated evaluation, proven cryptographic techniques, review of content inputs ).
Review and verify sources and citations in GAI system outputs during pre deployment risk measurement and ongoing monitoring activities.

mitigations.action_name: Maintain AI and software bill of materials
mitigations.description: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of components using Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). Evaluate AI BOMs and ML SBOMs starting with OWASP CycloneDX to ensure comprehensive tracking of all AI system dependencies.

mitigations.action_name: Use verifiable model sources with integrity checks
mitigations.description: Only use models from verifiable sources. Use third-party model integrity checks with signing and file hashes. Apply code signing for externally supplied code.
Define organizational responsibilities for periodic review of content provenance and incident monitoring for GAI systems.
Establish policies for measuring the effectiveness of employed content provenance methodologies (e.g., cryptography, watermarking, steganography, etc. )
Develop and validate approaches for measuring the success of content provenance management efforts with third parties (e.g., incidents detected and response times).
Maintain records of changes to content made by third parties to promote content provenance, including sources, timestamps, metadata.
Document training data sources to trace the origin and provenance of AI-generated content.

Evaluate feedback loops between GAI system content provenance and human reviewers, and update where needed. Implement real-time monitoring systems to affirm that cont e nt provenance protocols remain effective.
Use real-time auditing tools where they can be demonstrated to aid in the tracking and validation of the lineage and authenticity of AI-generated data.

Implement real-time monitoring processes for analyzing generated content performance and trustworthiness characteristics related to content provenance to identify deviations from the desired standards and trigger alerts for human intervention.
Track dataset modifications for provenance by monitoring data deletions, rectification requests, and other changes that may impact the verifiability of content origins.

Verify that AI Actors responsible for monitoring reported issues can effectively evaluate GAI system performance including the application of content provenance data tracking techniques, and promptly escalate issues for response.
Establish known assumptions and practices for determining data origin and content lineage, for documentation and evaluation purposes.
Identify and document how the system relies on upstream data sources, including for content provenance, and if it serves as an upstream dependency for other systems.
Observe and analyze how the GAI system interacts with external networks, and identify any potential for negative externalities, particularly where content provenance might be compromised.
Evaluate whether GAI operators and end-users can accurately understand content lineage and origin.
Apply TEVV practices for content provenance (e.g., probing a system's synthetic data generation capabilities for potential misuse or vulnerabilities .
Employ methods to trace the origin and modifications of digital content .
Integrate tools designed to analyze content provenance and detect data anomalies, verify the authenticity of digital signatures, and identify patterns associated with misinformation or manipulation.

Evaluate novel methods and technologies for the measurement of G AI-related risks in cluding in content provenance, offensive cyber, and CBRN, while maintaining the models' ability to produce valid, reliable, and factually accurate outputs.

Engage directly with end-users and other stakeholders to understand their expectations and concerns regarding content provenance. Use this feedback to guide the design of provenance data-tracking techniques.

Benchmark GAI system security and resilience related to content provenance against industry standards and best practices. Compare GAI system security features and content provenance methods against industry state-of-the-art.

Measure reliability of content authentication methods, such as watermarking, cryptographic signatures, digital fingerprints, as well as access controls, conformity assessment, and model integrity verification, which can help support the effective implementation of content provenance techniques. Evaluate the rate of false positives and false negatives in content provenance, as well as true positives and true negatives for verification.

Use digital content transparency solutions to enable the documentation of each instance where content is generated, modified, or shared to provide a tamper-proof history of the content, promote transparency, and enable traceability. Robust version control systems can also be applied to track chang es across the AI lifecycle over time.

Conduct studies to understand how end users perceive and interact with GAI content and accompanying content provenance within context of use. Assess whether the content aligns with their expectations and how they may act upon the information presented.

risks.threat: AI systems may operate with opaque decision-making processes that fail to meet the requirements for 'Appropriate Transparency and Explainability' outlined in the Trust AI policy.

risks.consequence: The inability to identify and correct errors in AI-generated code or decision outputs, and a failure to meet 'Contestability and Redress' standards.

mitigations.action_name: Incorporate differential privacy
mitigations.description: Apply differential privacy techniques that add calibrated noise to data or outputs, making reverse-engineering of individual data points difficult while preserving overall model utility.

mitigations.action_name: Test supplied models for tampering and poisoning
mitigations.description: Apply anomaly detection and adversarial robustness tests on supplied models and data to detect tampering and poisoning before integration into production systems.

mitigations.action_name: Track data origins and transformations
mitigations.description: Track data origins and transformations using tools like OWASP CycloneDX or ML-BOM. Verify data legitimacy across all stages of model development.

mitigations.action_name: Vet data vendors and validate outputs
mitigations.description: Vet data vendors rigorously. Validate model outputs against trusted sources to detect signs of poisoning or data manipulation.

mitigations.action_name: Sandbox model exposure to unverified data
mitigations.description: Implement strict sandboxing to limit model exposure to unverified data sources. Use anomaly detection to filter adversarial data before it enters the training pipeline.

mitigations.action_name: Use data version control
mitigations.description: Use data version control (DVC) to track changes in datasets and detect manipulation. Versioning is key to maintaining model integrity and enabling rollback if poisoning is detected.

mitigations.action_name: Red team for data poisoning robustness
mitigations.description: Test robustness via red team campaigns and adversarial methods such as federated learning approaches to minimize the impact of data perturbations on model behavior.

mitigations.action_name: Monitor training loss for poisoning indicators
mitigations.description: Monitor training loss and analyze model behavior for signs of poisoning. Use thresholds for detecting anomalous outputs that may indicate compromised training data.

mitigations.action_name: Validate knowledge base data integrity
mitigations.description: Implement robust data validation pipelines for knowledge sources. Regularly audit and verify knowledge base integrity for hidden codes, data poisoning, and adversarial embeddings. Only accept data from trusted and verified sources.
Test GAI system value chain risks (e.g., data poisoning, malware, other software and hardware vulnerabilities; labor practices; data privacy and localization compliance; geopolitical alignment).

Apply established security measures to: Assess likelihood and magnit ude of vulnerabilities and threats such as backdoors, compromised dependencies, data breaches, eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, reverse engineering, autonomous agents, model theft or exposure of model weights, AI inference, bypass, extraction, and other baseline security concerns.

Perform AI red-teaming to assess resilience against: Abuse to facilitate attacks on other systems (e.g., malicious code generation, enhanced phishing content), GAI attacks (e.g., prompt injection), ML attacks (e.g., adversarial examples/prompts, data poisoning, membership inference, model extraction, sponge examples).
Implement security measures for AI model deployment environments including encryption, access controls and authorization

mitigations.action_name: Train models for adversarial robustness against extraction
mitigations.description: Train models to detect and mitigate adversarial queries and model extraction attempts through adversarial robustness training techniques.
Engage in threat modeling to anticipate potential risks from GAI systems.
Collaborate with external researchers, industry experts, and community representatives to maintain awareness of emerging best practices and technologies in measuring and managing identified risks.
Implement plans for GAI systems to undergo regular adversarial testing to identify vulnerabilities and potential manipulation or misuse.
Conduct adversarial role-playing exercises, GAI red-teaming, or chaos testing to identify anomalous or unforeseen failure modes.
Verify that GAI system architecture can monitor outputs and performance, and handle, recover from, and repair errors when security anomalies, threats and impacts are detected.

Measure the rate at which recommendations from security checks and incidents are implemented. Assess how quickly the AI system can adapt and improve based on lessons learned from security incidents and feedback .
Regularly assess and verify that security measures remain been compromised.

Conduct adversarial testing at a regular cadence to map and measure GAI risks, including tests to address attempts to deceive or manipulate the application of provenance techniques or other misuses. Identify vulnerabilities and understand potential misuse scenarios and unintended outputs.
Implement adversarial testing program to validate system resilience against adversarial inputs and prompt injection attempts in line with adversarial threat taxonomy
Implement monitoring capabilities to detect and respond to adversarial inputs and prompt injection attempts

mitigations.action_name: Encrypt and verify models at AI edge
mitigations.description: Encrypt models deployed at AI edge with integrity checks. Use vendor attestation APIs to prevent tampered applications and models. Terminate applications running on unrecognized firmware.

mitigations.action_name: Limit exposure of logits and logprobs
mitigations.description: Restrict or obfuscate logit_bias and logprobs in API responses to prevent model extraction attacks that exploit token probability distributions.

mitigations.action_name: Implement output watermarking
mitigations.description: Implement watermarking frameworks to embed and detect unauthorized use of LLM outputs, enabling detection of model theft via output replication.

mitigations.action_name: Implement access controls for model repositories
mitigations.description: Implement strong access controls, including RBAC and least privilege, to limit unauthorized access to LLM model repositories and training environments, preventing model theft and tampering.

Conduct AI red-teaming to assess issues such as: Outputting of training data samples, and subsequent reverse engineering, model extraction, and membership inference risks; Revealing biometric, confidential, copyrighted, licensed, patented, personal, proprietary, sensitive, or trade-marked information ; Tracking or revealing location information of users or members of training datasets. Property

Identify metrics that reflect the effectiveness of security measures, such as data provenance, the number of unauthorized access attempts, inference, bypass, extraction, penetrations, or provenance verification.
Implement controls to prevent over-disclosure of technical information about AI systems and organizational details that could enable adversarial targeting
Implement safeguards to prevent probing or scraping of external AI endpoints
Document AI failure plan for AI privacy and security breaches assigning accountable owners and establishing notification and remediation with third-party support as needed (e.g. legal, PR, insurers)

mitigations.action_name: Treat model as untrusted user (zero-trust)
mitigations.description: Treat the model as any other user, adopting a zero-trust approach. Apply proper input validation on responses coming from the model to backend functions and downstream systems.

mitigations.action_name: Apply OWASP ASVS for output validation
mitigations.description: Follow OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) guidelines for effective input validation and sanitization of LLM-generated content before downstream processing.

mitigations.action_name: Encode model output to prevent code execution
mitigations.description: Encode model output back to users to mitigate undesired code execution by JavaScript or Markdown. Implement context-aware output encoding based on where the output will be used (HTML encoding for web, SQL escaping for databases).

mitigations.action_name: Use parameterized queries for LLM output
mitigations.description: Employ parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database operations involving LLM output to prevent SQL injection from model-generated content.

mitigations.action_name: Employ Content Security Policies for LLM content
mitigations.description: Employ strict Content Security Policies (CSP) to mitigate XSS attacks from LLM-generated content rendered in web applications.

mitigations.action_name: Establish secure coding practices for AI-generated code
mitigations.description: Establish secure coding practices and review processes to prevent integration of vulnerabilities due to incorrect code suggestions generated by LLMs.
Review GAI system outputs for validity and safety: Review generated code to assess risks that may arise from unreliable downstream decision-making.
Implement safeguards to prevent security vulnerabilities in outputs from impacting users
Implement or document guardrails to prevent AI-enabled misuse for cyber attacks and exploitation

mitigations.action_name: Constrain model behavior via system prompt
mitigations.description: Provide specific instructions about role, capabilities, and limitations in the system prompt. Enforce strict context adherence, limit responses to specific tasks and topics, and instruct the model to ignore modification attempts to its base instructions.

mitigations.action_name: Implement input and output filtering
mitigations.description: Define sensitive content categories and construct rules for identifying and handling such content. Apply semantic filters and string-checking to scan for non-allowed content. Evaluate responses using the RAG Triad (context relevance, groundedness, question/answer relevance).

mitigations.action_name: Conduct adversarial testing for prompt injection
mitigations.description: Perform regular penetration testing and breach simulations, treating the model as an untrusted user, to test trust boundaries and access control effectiveness against prompt injection attacks.

mitigations.action_name: Do not rely on system prompts for behavior control
mitigations.description: Avoid reliance on system prompts as the sole mechanism for strict behavior control. External systems should independently handle tasks like detecting and preventing harmful content rather than depending on prompt-based instructions.

Write 1-3 concise search queries. Each query should be a natural language description (1-2 sentences) using vocabulary that matches risk taxonomy entries.

- 5.4.1 Data Processing or Sharing Agreements (DPA) and Data Privacy Impact Assessments (DPIA) must be completed with regards to risk assessment and Data Sharing respectively. This includes but is not limited to documenting how the third party tool obtains, processes

- and stores data, who accesses it, when and why.  DPIAs require Information Governance sign-off.
- 5.4.2 Regulatory compliance: All development and procurement must take into account data privacy; consent (& opt out), surveillance concerns  [eg.RIPA] data sharing, intellectual property; equality of use; copyright law; FOI; etc.
- Accountability / Audit capabilities, including forensic evidence
- Data destruction/Subject Access Request
- Resilience
- Tools to report inaccurate data
- AI Data classification must be determined along with sensitivity (e.g. Identifiable; Anonymous; Synthetic data)
- Data aggregation risk must be evaluated as an AI tool may enable this tactic to be carried out much more easily than using traditional methods.
- 5.4.3 Data marked as Sensitive/Highly Sensitive or restricted must not be used in AI solutions unless wholly owned by the Trust and supported by appropriate contractual clauses.  Data traceability must be available.  Exceptions must be signed off by IG, IS and the IAO.
- 5.4.4 Ensure transparency regarding collection and processing of data, to include annotation, labelling, cleaning, enrichment, and aggregation.
- 5.4.5 For existing data sets to train the AI system, colleagues must assess the quantity and suitability of available data that will be needed by the system.
- 5.4.6 Regarding Large Language Models (LLMs)
- When registering to use an LLM for personal use, staff must not use their work (@gstt.nhs.uk or @nhs.net) email address. Any exception to this can only be done postDPIA approval, and for defined use case as agreed and documented in the DPIA
- LLMs are trained on massive datasets of text and code, and are still under development. They can sometimes generate incorrect or misleading information that can appear correct.
- LLMs should only be used for tasks that are appropriate for their capabilities.
- LLMs should not be used to make medical diagnoses or to provide medical advice if not approved for use as medical device.
- LLMs should be used in conjunction with other sources of information, such as medical textbooks and clinical guidelines.
- LLMs should be used with caution, and their output should always be verified via human intervention.

- The LLM itself may store and use the information entered into it insecurely or in a country where data protection laws are not in line with UK GDPR, which could lead to risk of GSTT not being compliant with data protection law or NHS value sharing frameworks. Scrutiny must be applied in this respect.
- Under no circumstances should personal identifiable or business sensitive information be entered in to the LLM. Only information that is already available in the public domain should be used. Unless data access and sharing can be appropriately restricted.
- 5.4.7  Refer to Information Governance Policies for further information on all wider Information Governance concepts.

Measures are required in the deployment and use of AI, for reasons including but not limited to: ensuring the safety of patients and the public and the protection of their rights; and upholding the Trust's probity with respect to legal obligations and standards of care. AI requires particular attention due to inherent complexities:
' The impact of AI on security depends on the way the technology is built and deployed; the complexity of the organisation deploying it; the strength and maturity of the existing risk management capabilities; and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing of personal data by the AI system, and the risks posed to individuals as a result ' [ICO]
'UK's approach to AI governance focuses on outcomes rather than the technology itself acknowledging that potential risks posed by AI will depend on the context of its application.' [UK Government]
The Trust must meet security requirements in line with the Trust and NHS information security policy and standards, laws and regulations, and contractual obligations. These include:
- UK Government / NHS /Trust policy as applicable to Artificial Intelligence in its various forms.
- UK Government guidance including ' Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK
1 UK Government guidance 'Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK Governnment' and Policy Whitepaper
- Governnment ' and Policy Whitepaper 'A pro -innovation approach to AI regulation'
- Trust Information Security Policy Framework
- General Data Protection Regulations (UK-GDPR) and Data Protection Act 2018
- Computer Misuse Act and Regulation of Investigatory Powers
- Network and Information Systems (NIS) regulations and NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT)
- Contractual agreements between The Trust and its third parties.
- Other accreditations where applicable, such as Payment Card Industry -Data Security Standards (PCi-DSS) and Cyber Essentials (CE/CE+)

queries: Unauthorized access, data breaches, or exploitation of AI system vulnerabilities leading to threats to patient safety and public security
Non-compliance with data protection laws, including unauthorized processing or exposure of personal and sensitive data during AI operations
Risks to individual rights and safety arising from the deployment of complex AI systems in sensitive healthcare contexts

- 5.5.1 AI tooling must never be used to circumvent security controls at the Trust.  (For example hacking devices, jailbreak, eavesdropping, etc).
- 5.5.2 The Trust will perform regular audits and monitoring of public AI tools, including ChatGPT, GenAI and other LLMs to further enhance data security. The Trust may decide to limit
- access to these tools to specific employees or teams, based on their job roles and responsibilities.
- 5.5.3 Content filtering may be implemented based on Trust data classification and labelling rules to guard against inappropriate content generated by employees.
- 5.5.4 Any AI integration with Trust systems or using Trust credentials must go through Demand/Non-Standard Demand process and be approved by Information Security.
- 5.5.5 Security tooling may make use AI or Machine Learning, provided that use cases are justified and approved by Information Security.  This includes but is not limited to security incident resolution, device management, risk assessment.
- Where tooling is cloud-based, Trust policies apply.
- AI security tools must not use Trust data for their machine learning models
- AI security tools must be supported by a contract between the Trust and the vendor.
- 5.5.6 The Trust must guard against security risks specific to AI solutions, including but not limited to:
- Personal data of users of the AI system being inadvertently revealed by the outputs of the system itself.
- Malicious Self-replicating prompts (worms in GenAI ecosystems 2 ) and other GenAI ecosystem compromise
- Model inversion attacks
- Membership inference attacks
- White/Black box attacks
- Adversarial examples
- Misinformation spread

This policy is for Information Governance and Information Security aspects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.  The UK government highlights aspects of infrastructure for AI development and deployment that require assurance. These include 1 :
- Training Data
- AI Models
- AI Systems
- Broader Operational Context
The scope of this policy is Information Security and Information Governance within AI systems used at the Trust, to enable a risk-based approach to Artificial Intelligence that fits within the Information Security Policy Framework, Information Governance Policy, and Trust AI requirements.
Some examples of AI enabled systems are listed below, this list is not exhaustive.
- Generative AI - including Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT.
- o An LLM is a type of artificial intelligence (AI) program that can recognise and generate text, among other tasks. LLMs are trained on huge sets of data -hence the name "large." LLMs are built on machine learning: specifically, a type of neural network called a transformer model.
- Automated healthcare triage systems
- AI enabled tools (e.g. Microsoft PowerApps/Security enforcing systems and tooling/Chatbots)
- Natural language processing, computer vision, neural networks and distributed artificial intelligence
- AI as a medical device (e.g. where the AI has some functionally diagnostic output that has a dosing implication).
Out of scope: Robotic process automation, which although is non-human based processing, is programmatic, deterministic software and are not generally considered Artificial Intelligence. Information Governance and Security policies still apply.

queries: Unauthorized access, leakage, or exposure of sensitive training data and personal information during AI model development and deployment
Security vulnerabilities and exploitation of AI models, systems, and infrastructure, including prompt injection and adversarial attacks
Risks associated with AI-driven clinical decisions, including diagnostic errors and incorrect dosing implications in AI as a medical device

- Under no circumstances should personal identifiable or business sensitive information be entered into a Large Language Model (LLM) or publicly available Artificial Intelligence (AI) solution. This includes but is not limited to: Sensitive information; Patient Information; Staff Information; Intellectual Property; Proprietary Code or proprietary information; Passwords; Keys; credit card numbers or other financial information.
- o Only information that is already available in the public domain should be used, unless data access and sharing can be locked down and guaranteed via contractual clauses.
- Trust Login Accounts must not be used for public AI tools such as ChatGPT etc.
- Staff must not use their work (gstt.nhs.uk;rbht.nhs.uk; nhs.net) email address when registering to use an LLM for personal use.
- Don't assume AI security tooling can replace a zero-trust security strategy; Role Based Access Control and Least Privilege must still apply.
- Don't install or use a solution that will require an unauthorised change to Trust systems including desktops, firewall rules, etc.
- Don't install or use a solution that would circumvent Trust policies and standards.
- Don't integrate any AI technology with Trust systems without the correct due diligence and approval.
- DO remember that all Trust policies and standards apply to AI solutions, whether they are proofof-concept (POC) or permanent implementations.
- Remember that an LLM itself may store the information entered into it insecurely or in a country where data protection laws are not in line with UK GDPR, which put GSTT at risk of not being compliant with UK data protection law. Ensure tools comply with all data protection regulations
- Always use LLMs with caution.
- Be aware that LLMs are trained on massive datasets of text and code, are still under development, and they can sometimes generate incorrect or misleading information.
- LLM output must always be verified via human intervention.
- Output from LLMs should be validated and correlated with other trusted sources of information. Fact-check all content.  False positives and negatives do occur.
- DO make sure that user Least Privilege and RBAC are incorporated into the solution.
- Treat the information entered into public AI solutions as if you are posting on a public website.

- Remember that providers can and do monitor conversations to improve their systems and ensure the content complies with their own policies and safety requirements. There are no known assurances regarding their employees, contractors or partners who may view the information you post.  Bear this in mind to prevent a data breach of sensitive information.
- Use Multi-Factor authentication.
- AI prompts should be documented and standardised.
- Ensure that adversarial scenarios are tested against solutions to ensure resilience in the face of manipulative attacks.
- Do ensure when solutions and POCs are retired that all data models are securely deleted along with the data itself, as per Trust retention and trust data destruction standards.  Documentation of these actions must be retained as part of any project.
- When developing AI, make sure that Disaster Recovery and Resilience is considered at solution design stage.

queries: Unauthorized disclosure, leakage, or exposure of PII, sensitive medical data, intellectual property, or credentials through LLM prompts and training data
AI-generated hallucinations, misinformation, and the production of incorrect or misleading content requiring human verification

- 5.4.1 Data Processing or Sharing Agreements (DPA) and Data Privacy Impact Assessments (DPIA) must be completed with regards to risk assessment and Data Sharing respectively. This includes but is not limited to documenting how the third party tool obtains, processes

- and stores data, who accesses it, when and why.  DPIAs require Information Governance sign-off.

- Resilience

- 5.4.4 Ensure transparency regarding collection and processing of data, to include annotation, labelling, cleaning, enrichment, and aggregation.
- 5.4.5 For existing data sets to train the AI system, colleagues must assess the quantity and suitability of available data that will be needed by the system.
- 5.4.6 Regarding Large Language Models (LLMs)
- When registering to use an LLM for personal use, staff must not use their work (@gstt.nhs.uk or @nhs.net) email address. Any exception to this can only be done postDPIA approval, and for defined use case as agreed and documented in the DPIA
- LLMs are trained on massive datasets of text and code, and are still under development. They can sometimes generate incorrect or misleading information that can appear correct.
- LLMs should only be used for tasks that are appropriate for their capabilities.
- LLMs should not be used to make medical diagnoses or to provide medical advice if not approved for use as medical device.
- LLMs should be used in conjunction with other sources of information, such as medical textbooks and clinical guidelines.
- LLMs should be used with caution, and their output should always be verified via human intervention.

- The LLM itself may store and use the information entered into it insecurely or in a country where data protection laws are not in line with UK GDPR, which could lead to risk of GSTT not being compliant with data protection law or NHS value sharing frameworks. Scrutiny must be applied in this respect.
- Under no circumstances should personal identifiable or business sensitive information be entered in to the LLM. Only information that is already available in the public domain should be used. Unless data access and sharing can be appropriately restricted.

## 1 Scope

This policy is for Information Governance and Information Security aspects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.  The UK government highlights aspects of infrastructure for AI development and deployment that require assurance. These include 1 :
- Training Data
- AI Models
- AI Systems
- Broader Operational Context
The scope of this policy is Information Security and Information Governance within AI systems used at the Trust, to enable a risk-based approach to Artificial Intelligence that fits within the Information Security Policy Framework, Information Governance Policy, and Trust AI requirements.
Some examples of AI enabled systems are listed below, this list is not exhaustive.
- Generative AI - including Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT.
- o An LLM is a type of artificial intelligence (AI) program that can recognise and generate text, among other tasks. LLMs are trained on huge sets of data -hence the name "large." LLMs are built on machine learning: specifically, a type of neural network called a transformer model.
- Automated healthcare triage systems
- AI enabled tools (e.g. Microsoft PowerApps/Security enforcing systems and tooling/Chatbots)
- Natural language processing, computer vision, neural networks and distributed artificial intelligence
- AI as a medical device (e.g. where the AI has some functionally diagnostic output that has a dosing implication).
Out of scope: Robotic process automation, which although is non-human based processing, is programmatic, deterministic software and are not generally considered Artificial Intelligence. Information Governance and Security policies still apply.

## 2 Rationale

Measures are required in the deployment and use of AI, for reasons including but not limited to: ensuring the safety of patients and the public and the protection of their rights; and upholding the Trust's probity with respect to legal obligations and standards of care. AI requires particular attention due to inherent complexities:
' The impact of AI on security depends on the way the technology is built and deployed; the complexity of the organisation deploying it; the strength and maturity of the existing risk management capabilities; and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing of personal data by the AI system, and the risks posed to individuals as a result ' [ICO]
'UK's approach to AI governance focuses on outcomes rather than the technology itself acknowledging that potential risks posed by AI will depend on the context of its application.' [UK Government]
The Trust must meet security requirements in line with the Trust and NHS information security policy and standards, laws and regulations, and contractual obligations. These include:
- UK Government / NHS /Trust policy as applicable to Artificial Intelligence in its various forms.
- UK Government guidance including ' Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK
1 UK Government guidance 'Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK Governnment' and Policy Whitepaper
- Governnment ' and Policy Whitepaper 'A pro -innovation approach to AI regulation'
- Trust Information Security Policy Framework
- General Data Protection Regulations (UK-GDPR) and Data Protection Act 2018
- Computer Misuse Act and Regulation of Investigatory Powers
- Network and Information Systems (NIS) regulations and NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT)
- Contractual agreements between The Trust and its third parties.
- Other accreditations where applicable, such as Payment Card Industry -Data Security Standards (PCi-DSS) and Cyber Essentials (CE/CE+)

## 3.1 This policy is intended to:

- Ensure Information Security and Information Governance is embedded for any use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.
- Provide security/governance guidance to any user wishing to use AI tools.
- Ensure only appropriate people will access information across the AI lifecycle.
- Enhance Security Awareness around malicious AI use cases.
- o For example, AI can be used by cybercriminals to generate phishing emails, malicious code, QR codes, deepfake video / audio, malware, internet scraping, to obtain credentials for hacking accounts, exfiltrating sensitive Trust data (e.g. personal, patient or financial information), or to evade detection.
- Embed AI security into the Trust risk management framework.
- This policy does not cover all aspects of the governance and strategic oversight of AI.
- 3.2 Other sources of authority in Trust policy include:
- The Trust's overarching Medical Device Policy and subtending policy documents, govern considerations of AI as a medical device and its governance in use, as aligned with Medical Devices Regulations, including the requirement for CE/UKCA.  For example, Trustdeveloped solutions that are shared with colleagues outside the Trust may constitute 'placing on the market' under the MDR, and therefore require CE/UKCA marking.
- This Trust's R&D policy governs aspects of research applied to AI .

## Candidate Risks

- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-collection/gathering/stealing**: Unauthorized collection/gathering/stealing (9 variants) — Unauthorized collection/gathering/stealing: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized collection/gathering/stealing across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).
- **credo-risk-038**: Compromised confidential information (Slattery et al., 2024; IBM, 2024;AI, 2023) — The AI system, including its supporting compute infrastructure, may serve as an attack vector for intrusion into cyber-physical or cloud environments, or enable exfiltration of secrets.
- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-disclosure**: Unauthorized disclosure (9 variants) — Unauthorized disclosure: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized disclosure across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).
- **atlas-legal-accountability**: Legal accountability — Determining who is responsible for an AI model is challenging without good documentation and governance processes. The use of synthetic data in model development adds further complexity, since the lack of standardized frameworks for recording synthetic data design choices and verification steps makes accountability harder to establish.
- **atlas-attribute-inference-attack**: Attribute inference attack — An attribute inference attack repeatedly queries a model to detect whether certain sensitive features can be inferred about individuals who participated in training a model. These attacks occur when an adversary has some prior knowledge about the training data and uses that knowledge to infer the sensitive data.
- **atlas-prompt-priming**: Prompt priming — Because generative models produce output based on the input provided, the model can be prompted to reveal specific kinds of information. For example, adding personal information in the prompt increases its likelihood of generating similar kinds of personal information in its output. If personal data was included as part of the model's training, there is a possibility it could be revealed.
- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-inference/synthesis**: Unauthorized inference/synthesis (9 variants) — Unauthorized inference/synthesis: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized inference/synthesis across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).
- **atlas-data-usage**: Data usage restrictions — Laws and other restrictions can limit or prohibit the use of some data for specific AI use cases.
- **atlas-data-acquisition**: Data acquisition restrictions — Laws and other regulations might limit the collection of certain types of data for specific AI use cases.
- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-processing**: Unauthorized processing (9 variants) — Unauthorized processing: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized processing across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).

The policy explicitly aims to ensure the 'Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability of Trust data' and addresses the risk of AI being used to 'exfiltrate sensitive Trust data', which aligns with the risk of compromised confidential information and exfiltration of secrets.

The policy addresses the protection of 'personal, patient or financial information' and the need to ensure 'only appropriate people will access information across the AI lifecycle', which is a direct management of unauthorized disclosure risks.

The text establishes a governance framework including an 'Approving body' (Trust Risk & Assurance Committee), 'Owners', and 'Responsible Leads', and explicitly mentions meeting 'legal obligations', 'laws and regulations', and 'contractual obligations', all of which are central to establishing legal accountability.

While the text discusses data protection and AI models, it does not specifically mention or describe the technical mechanism of attribute inference attacks or the querying of models to detect sensitive features.
The text mentions Generative AI and LLMs, but it does not specifically address the risk of prompt priming or the manipulation of prompts to reveal training data.
The text focuses on security, governance, and data protection, but it does not specifically address the risk of unauthorized inference or the synthesis of new data from existing datasets.
The policy explicitly references compliance with 'UK-GDPR', 'Data Protection Act 2018', and 'contractual obligations', which are the primary drivers for managing data usage restrictions.

The text mentions the need to comply with 'laws and regulations' (like GDPR) and 'contractual agreements' regarding the processing of personal data, which inherently encompasses the legal restrictions on how data is acquired/collected for AI.

The text explicitly mentions the 'nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing of personal data' and aims to ensure 'Information Governance' is embedded, which is the management of unauthorized processing risks.

- 5.2.1 All solutions must follow Architecture and Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) best practice, and a High Level Design (HLD) must be produced.
- 5.2.2 When procuring AI solutions, terms and conditions must be clearly reviewed and ensure that they align with the Trust security standards.
- Appropriate and relevant Security risk assessments must be completed before procurement.
- Appropriate and relevant general Information Governance measures must be included in contracts to support the project including relevant DPIAs which must be signed off by Information Governance.
- Appropriate and relevant Technical security / organisational measures must be included in contracts to ensure security by design.  See Trust Third Party Security Policy for further information.
- 5.2.3 When developing AI solutions, Trust policy regarding risk management, data protection, security assurance, vulnerability management and penetration testing applies. See Vulnerability Management Policy for more information.
- When using AI tools in system development, it must not be assumed that the AI generated code is inherently more secure.  Code should be static and dynamically tested to ensure secure coding has been achieved.
- See Information Governance policies for further general guidance regarding use of Trust data.
- 5.2.4 For further guidance on all Trust-Developed or Third Party solutions, refer to ' Introduction to
AI Assurance (Guidance) UK Governnment ' (reference 1, section 9)  and Trust AI policy to review aspects of AI systems outside of IG/IS remit including but not limited to:
- Safety and Robustness
- Appropriate Transparency and Explainability
- Fairness
- Accountability
- Contestability and Redress
- Justified Trust
- Benefits e.g. competitive advantage, research, etc.
- Cross-border considerations
- Evaluation and AI Lifecycle including emerging trends
- AI Assurance Landscape including data quality and decision making

## 5.3 Operation and Monitoring

- 5.3.1 AI solutions must be monitored for security purposes.
Monitoring methods may be diverse, since 'AI solutions' includes technologies ranging from Generative AI - including Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Open Source systems, and API traffic. Monitoring procedures may include but not be limited to:
- Monitoring for AI specific attacks (e.g. generate phishing emails; malicious code; QR Codes; Deepfakes; malware; scrape internet; to obtain credentials, personal Data or financial information; or evade detection) will be carried out.
- o See Appendix A for information regarding risk assessment and countermeasures.
- Data Loss Prevention (DLP) monitoring will be applied as available, based on Trust data classification, labelling, and in line with records management.
- 5.3.2 Biometric data for user logins/identification (as defined by UK GDPR Article 4.14) must not be used for any AI technology within Trust-owned solutions. See Reference 8 (section 9 of this document) for further context.
- Personal devices, however, may require extra security.  Please refer to the Personal Device (BYOD) policy for recommendations on biometric authentication on a personal device.
- 5.3.3 Refer to 'Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK Governnment' and Trust AI policy for further guidance on:
- Managing bias
- Socio-economic implications
- Robot accounts (incl Chatbots)
- Image recognition
- Appendix A and B for additional context
- 5.3.4 As per the System Access Management Security Policy, AI solutions must have stakeholders who are responsible and accountable for troubleshooting, managing, operating, overseeing, and controlling the system. This typically would be the Information Asset Owner.

## 5.4 Information Governance and Resilience

- 5.4.1 Data Processing or Sharing Agreements (DPA) and Data Privacy Impact Assessments (DPIA) must be completed with regards to risk assessment and Data Sharing respectively. This includes but is not limited to documenting how the third party tool obtains, processes

- and stores data, who accesses it, when and why.  DPIAs require Information Governance sign-off.
- 5.4.2 Regulatory compliance: All development and procurement must take into account data privacy; consent (& opt out), surveillance concerns  [eg.RIPA] data sharing, intellectual property; equality of use; copyright law; FOI; etc.
- Accountability / Audit capabilities, including forensic evidence
- Data destruction/Subject Access Request
- Resilience
- Tools to report inaccurate data

- Data aggregation risk must be evaluated as an AI tool may enable this tactic to be carried out much more easily than using traditional methods.

- 5.4.5 For existing data sets to train the AI system, colleagues must assess the quantity and suitability of available data that will be needed by the system.
- 5.4.6 Regarding Large Language Models (LLMs)

- LLMs are trained on massive datasets of text and code, and are still under development. They can sometimes generate incorrect or misleading information that can appear correct.

## 1 Scope

This policy is for Information Governance and Information Security aspects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.  The UK government highlights aspects of infrastructure for AI development and deployment that require assurance. These include 1 :
- Training Data
- AI Models
- AI Systems
- Broader Operational Context
The scope of this policy is Information Security and Information Governance within AI systems used at the Trust, to enable a risk-based approach to Artificial Intelligence that fits within the Information Security Policy Framework, Information Governance Policy, and Trust AI requirements.
Some examples of AI enabled systems are listed below, this list is not exhaustive.
- Generative AI - including Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT.
- o An LLM is a type of artificial intelligence (AI) program that can recognise and generate text, among other tasks. LLMs are trained on huge sets of data -hence the name "large." LLMs are built on machine learning: specifically, a type of neural network called a transformer model.
- Automated healthcare triage systems
- AI enabled tools (e.g. Microsoft PowerApps/Security enforcing systems and tooling/Chatbots)

## 1 Scope

This policy is for Information Governance and Information Security aspects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.  The UK government highlights aspects of infrastructure for AI development and deployment that require assurance. These include 1 :
- Training Data
- AI Models
- AI Systems
- Broader Operational Context
The scope of this policy is Information Security and Information Governance within AI systems used at the Trust, to enable a risk-based approach to Artificial Intelligence that fits within the Information Security Policy Framework, Information Governance Policy, and Trust AI requirements.
Some examples of AI enabled systems are listed below, this list is not exhaustive.
- Generative AI - including Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT.
- o An LLM is a type of artificial intelligence (AI) program that can recognise and generate text, among other tasks. LLMs are trained on huge sets of data -hence the name "large." LLMs are built on machine learning: specifically, a type of neural network called a transformer model.
- Automated healthcare triage systems
- AI enabled tools (e.g. Microsoft PowerApps/Security enforcing systems and tooling/Chatbots)
- Natural language processing, computer vision, neural networks and distributed artificial intelligence
- AI as a medical device (e.g. where the AI has some functionally diagnostic output that has a dosing implication).
Out of scope: Robotic process automation, which although is non-human based processing, is programmatic, deterministic software and are not generally considered Artificial Intelligence. Information Governance and Security policies still apply.

## 2 Rationale

Measures are required in the deployment and use of AI, for reasons including but not limited to: ensuring the safety of patients and the public and the protection of their rights; and upholding the Trust's probity with respect to legal obligations and standards of care. AI requires particular attention due to inherent complexities:
' The impact of AI on security depends on the way the technology is built and deployed; the complexity of the organisation deploying it; the strength and maturity of the existing risk management capabilities; and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing of personal data by the AI system, and the risks posed to individuals as a result ' [ICO]
'UK's approach to AI governance focuses on outcomes rather than the technology itself acknowledging that potential risks posed by AI will depend on the context of its application.' [UK Government]
The Trust must meet security requirements in line with the Trust and NHS information security policy and standards, laws and regulations, and contractual obligations. These include:
- UK Government / NHS /Trust policy as applicable to Artificial Intelligence in its various forms.
- UK Government guidance including ' Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK
1 UK Government guidance 'Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK Governnment' and Policy Whitepaper
- Governnment ' and Policy Whitepaper 'A pro -innovation approach to AI regulation'
- Trust Information Security Policy Framework
- General Data Protection Regulations (UK-GDPR) and Data Protection Act 2018
- Computer Misuse Act and Regulation of Investigatory Powers
- Network and Information Systems (NIS) regulations and NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT)
- Contractual agreements between The Trust and its third parties.
- Other accreditations where applicable, such as Payment Card Industry -Data Security Standards (PCi-DSS) and Cyber Essentials (CE/CE+)

## 3.1 This policy is intended to:

- Ensure Information Security and Information Governance is embedded for any use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.
- Provide security/governance guidance to any user wishing to use AI tools.
- Ensure only appropriate people will access information across the AI lifecycle.
- Enhance Security Awareness around malicious AI use cases.
- o For example, AI can be used by cybercriminals to generate phishing emails, malicious code, QR codes, deepfake video / audio, malware, internet scraping, to obtain credentials for hacking accounts, exfiltrating sensitive Trust data (e.g. personal, patient or financial information), or to evade detection.
- Embed AI security into the Trust risk management framework.
- This policy does not cover all aspects of the governance and strategic oversight of AI.
- 3.2 Other sources of authority in Trust policy include:
- The Trust's overarching Medical Device Policy and subtending policy documents, govern considerations of AI as a medical device and its governance in use, as aligned with Medical Devices Regulations, including the requirement for CE/UKCA.  For example, Trustdeveloped solutions that are shared with colleagues outside the Trust may constitute 'placing on the market' under the MDR, and therefore require CE/UKCA marking.
- This Trust's R&D policy governs aspects of research applied to AI .

## Candidate risks

- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-disclosure** (Unauthorized disclosure (9 variants)): Unauthorized disclosure: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized disclosure across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).

- 5.6.1 Trust Policy applies.  Data breaches involving any AI tool, including Trust developed and third party solutions, must be reported promptly via the Trust Incident Management reporting system (RADAR).  This will cascade relevant notification to appropriate groups (e.g. IG and IS)
- 5.6.2 Any request to input Trust data into public tools must be reviewed by IG and IS on a case by case basis, and must be supported by contractual clause within the vendor contract.
Input of Trust sensitive and proprietary data outside of those approved in 5.6.2 into public, free or publicly available AI tools such as ChatGPT or OSINT tools will be considered a data breach.

## 7  Education and other considerations

There are other considerations which may have an indirect impact on the Trust Information Governance or Information Security landscape.

## 7.1  Education

The following points apply to staff undertaking internal education courses and as part of their programme are required to submit competency documents and academic writing:
- AI tools have the potential to enhance learning, and can support inclusivity and accessibility when used appropriately. It is important that you understand the potential risks and benefits of these tools if you plan to use them during your studies.
- You may use AI tools like any other resource to help you generate ideas, key themes, and plan your assessment.
2  Here Comes The AI Worm: Unleashing Zero-click Worms that Target GenAI-Powered Applications Stav Cohen, Ron Bitton, Ben Nassi, Cornell University
- Factual evidence, including quotes and referencing must come from trusted sources.
- Passing off work generated by AI is not acceptable, and will be treated as seriously as plagiarism.
- Some courses or assignments may vary this position. In these cases you will be given detailed instructions on what is and isn't allowed, and may be asked to sign a code of conduct.
- If you are unclear about what is permissible, contact the course lead.

## 7.2  Other Considerations

- Power consumption used by AI tools may have operational impact.
- Other nations legislation regarding use of AI should also be considered. (EU/US/China etc..) For example, the EU AI Act is referenced in section 9 of this document (reference 5).

## 8 Do's and Don'ts

- Under no circumstances should personal identifiable or business sensitive information be entered into a Large Language Model (LLM) or publicly available Artificial Intelligence (AI) solution. This includes but is not limited to: Sensitive information; Patient Information; Staff Information; Intellectual Property; Proprietary Code or proprietary information; Passwords; Keys; credit card numbers or other financial information.
- o Only information that is already available in the public domain should be used, unless data access and sharing can be locked down and guaranteed via contractual clauses.
- Trust Login Accounts must not be used for public AI tools such as ChatGPT etc.
- Staff must not use their work (gstt.nhs.uk;rbht.nhs.uk; nhs.net) email address when registering to use an LLM for personal use.
- Don't assume AI security tooling can replace a zero-trust security strategy; Role Based Access Control and Least Privilege must still apply.
- Don't install or use a solution that will require an unauthorised change to Trust systems including desktops, firewall rules, etc.
- Don't install or use a solution that would circumvent Trust policies and standards.
- Don't integrate any AI technology with Trust systems without the correct due diligence and approval.
- DO remember that all Trust policies and standards apply to AI solutions, whether they are proofof-concept (POC) or permanent implementations.
- Remember that an LLM itself may store the information entered into it insecurely or in a country where data protection laws are not in line with UK GDPR, which put GSTT at risk of not being compliant with UK data protection law. Ensure tools comply with all data protection regulations
- Always use LLMs with caution.
- Be aware that LLMs are trained on massive datasets of text and code, are still under development, and they can sometimes generate incorrect or misleading information.
- LLM output must always be verified via human intervention.
- Output from LLMs should be validated and correlated with other trusted sources of information. Fact-check all content.  False positives and negatives do occur.
- DO make sure that user Least Privilege and RBAC are incorporated into the solution.
- Treat the information entered into public AI solutions as if you are posting on a public website.

- Remember that providers can and do monitor conversations to improve their systems and ensure the content complies with their own policies and safety requirements. There are no known assurances regarding their employees, contractors or partners who may view the information you post.  Bear this in mind to prevent a data breach of sensitive information.
- Use Multi-Factor authentication.
- AI prompts should be documented and standardised.
- Ensure that adversarial scenarios are tested against solutions to ensure resilience in the face of manipulative attacks.
- Do ensure when solutions and POCs are retired that all data models are securely deleted along with the data itself, as per Trust retention and trust data destruction standards.  Documentation of these actions must be retained as part of any project.
- When developing AI, make sure that Disaster Recovery and Resilience is considered at solution design stage.

## 8 Monitoring and Assurance

- **mit-ai-risk-subdomain-6.6** (Environmental harm): The development and operation of AI systems causing environmental harm, such as through energy consumption of data centers, or material and carbon footprints associated with AI hardware.

## 1 Scope

This policy is for Information Governance and Information Security aspects of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.  The UK government highlights aspects of infrastructure for AI development and deployment that require assurance. These include 1 :
- Training Data
- AI Models
- AI Systems
- Broader Operational Context
The scope of this policy is Information Security and Information Governance within AI systems used at the Trust, to enable a risk-based approach to Artificial Intelligence that fits within the Information Security Policy Framework, Information Governance Policy, and Trust AI requirements.
Some examples of AI enabled systems are listed below, this list is not exhaustive.
- Generative AI - including Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT.
- o An LLM is a type of artificial intelligence (AI) program that can recognise and generate text, among other tasks. LLMs are trained on huge sets of data -hence the name "large." LLMs are built on machine learning: specifically, a type of neural network called a transformer model.
- Automated healthcare triage systems
- AI enabled tools (e.g. Microsoft PowerApps/Security enforcing systems and tooling/Chatbots)
- Natural language processing, computer vision, neural networks and distributed artificial intelligence
- AI as a medical device (e.g. where the AI has some functionally diagnostic output that has a dosing implication).
Out of scope: Robotic process automation, which although is non-human based processing, is programmatic, deterministic software and are not generally considered Artificial Intelligence. Information Governance and Security policies still apply.

## 2 Rationale

Measures are required in the deployment and use of AI, for reasons including but not limited to: ensuring the safety of patients and the public and the protection of their rights; and upholding the Trust's probity with respect to legal obligations and standards of care. AI requires particular attention due to inherent complexities:
' The impact of AI on security depends on the way the technology is built and deployed; the complexity of the organisation deploying it; the strength and maturity of the existing risk management capabilities; and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing of personal data by the AI system, and the risks posed to individuals as a result ' [ICO]
'UK's approach to AI governance focuses on outcomes rather than the technology itself acknowledging that potential risks posed by AI will depend on the context of its application.' [UK Government]
The Trust must meet security requirements in line with the Trust and NHS information security policy and standards, laws and regulations, and contractual obligations. These include:
- UK Government / NHS /Trust policy as applicable to Artificial Intelligence in its various forms.
- UK Government guidance including ' Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK
1 UK Government guidance 'Introduction to AI Assurance (Guidance) UK Governnment' and Policy Whitepaper
- Governnment ' and Policy Whitepaper 'A pro -innovation approach to AI regulation'
- Trust Information Security Policy Framework
- General Data Protection Regulations (UK-GDPR) and Data Protection Act 2018
- Computer Misuse Act and Regulation of Investigatory Powers
- Network and Information Systems (NIS) regulations and NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit (DSPT)
- Contractual agreements between The Trust and its third parties.
- Other accreditations where applicable, such as Payment Card Industry -Data Security Standards (PCi-DSS) and Cyber Essentials (CE/CE+)

## 3.1 This policy is intended to:

- Ensure Information Security and Information Governance is embedded for any use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) at the Trust.
- Provide security/governance guidance to any user wishing to use AI tools.
- Ensure only appropriate people will access information across the AI lifecycle.
- Enhance Security Awareness around malicious AI use cases.
- o For example, AI can be used by cybercriminals to generate phishing emails, malicious code, QR codes, deepfake video / audio, malware, internet scraping, to obtain credentials for hacking accounts, exfiltrating sensitive Trust data (e.g. personal, patient or financial information), or to evade detection.
- Embed AI security into the Trust risk management framework.
- This policy does not cover all aspects of the governance and strategic oversight of AI.
- 3.2 Other sources of authority in Trust policy include:
- The Trust's overarching Medical Device Policy and subtending policy documents, govern considerations of AI as a medical device and its governance in use, as aligned with Medical Devices Regulations, including the requirement for CE/UKCA.  For example, Trustdeveloped solutions that are shared with colleagues outside the Trust may constitute 'placing on the market' under the MDR, and therefore require CE/UKCA marking.
- This Trust's R&D policy governs aspects of research applied to AI .

## Candidate risks

- **credo-risk-037** (Compromised sensitive information (Slattery et al., 2024; IBM, 2024; AI, 2023)): The AI system may expose personally sensitive information, either inadvertently or due to adversarial inputs, derived from training data, accessible data, or inferences. Sensitive personal data is information that, while not necessarily identifying an individual, could cause harm, discrimination, or distress to a person if exposed, including details about their health, finances, beliefs, behaviors, relationships, and private life circumstances.
- **credo-risk-041** (Vulnerability to adversarial attacks (Slattery et al., 2024; IBM, 2024; AI, 2023)): The AI system may be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, including prompt-based attacks, which may induce the model to behave outside of its intended functionality.
- **credo-risk-036** (Compromised personally identifiable information (Slattery et al., 2024)): The AI system may expose personally identifiable information (PII), either inadvertently or due to adversarial inputs, derived from training data, accessible data, or inferences. PII is any data that can be used to directly identify or contact a specific individual, either alone or in combination with other information.
- **mit-ai-risk-subdomain-2.2** (AI system security vulnerabilities and attacks): Vulnerabilities in AI systems, software development toolchains, and hardware that can be exploited, resulting in unauthorized access, data and privacy breaches, or system manipulation causing unsafe outputs or behavior.
- **atlas-exposing-personal-information** (Exposing personal information): When personal identifiable information (PII) or sensitive personal information (SPI) are used in training data, fine-tuning data, seed data for synthetic data generation, or as part of the prompt, models might reveal that data in the generated output. Revealing personal information is a type of data leakage.
- **credo-risk-040** (AI-generated security weaknesses (Slattery et al., 2024; IBM, 2024; AI, 2023)): AI system security vulnerabilities: Implementation weaknesses in AI system architecture and infrastructure
- **atlas-personal-information-in-data** (Personal information in data): Inclusion or presence of personal identifiable information (PII) and sensitive personal information (SPI) in the data used for training or fine tuning the model might result in unwanted disclosure of that information.
- **mit-ai-risk-subdomain-2.1** (Compromise of privacy by obtaining, leaking or correctly inferring sensitive information): AI systems that memorize and leak sensitive personal data or infer private information about individuals without their consent. Unexpected or unauthorized sharing of data and information can compromise user expectation of privacy, assist identity theft, or loss of confidential intellectual property.
- **atlas-revealing-confidential-information** (Revealing confidential information): When confidential information is used in training data, fine-tuning data, or as part of the prompt, models might reveal that data in the generated output. Revealing confidential information is a type of data leakage.
- **credo-risk-039** (AI model and intellectual property theft): AI model and intellectual property theft - Unauthorized copying of trained models and associated AI intellectual property
- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-collection/gathering/stealing** (Unauthorized collection/gathering/stealing (9 variants)): Unauthorized collection/gathering/stealing: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized collection/gathering/stealing across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).
- **credo-risk-038** (Compromised confidential information (Slattery et al., 2024; IBM, 2024;AI, 2023)): The AI system, including its supporting compute infrastructure, may serve as an attack vector for intrusion into cyber-physical or cloud environments, or enable exfiltration of secrets.
- **ai-risk-taxonomy-unauthorized-disclosure** (Unauthorized disclosure (9 variants)): Unauthorized disclosure: risk of AI systems involving unauthorized disclosure across categories including Behavioral/ Preference data, Biometric data (facial recognition), Communication Records, Demographic data, Educational records, Financial records, Health data, Location data, PII (Personal Identifiable Information).
- **atlas-legal-accountability** (Legal accountability): Determining who is responsible for an AI model is challenging without good documentation and governance processes. The use of synthetic data in model development adds further complexity, since the lack of standardized frameworks for recording synthetic data design choices and verification steps makes accountability harder to establish.
- **atlas-data-usage** (Data usage restrictions): Laws and other restrictions can limit or prohibit the use of some data for specific AI use cases.
- **atlas-data-acquisition** (Data acquisition restrictions): Laws and other regulations might limit the collection of certain types of data for specific AI use cases.

## 8 Do's and Don'ts

- Under no circumstances should personal identifiable or business sensitive information be entered into a Large Language Model (LLM) or publicly available Artificial Intelligence (AI) solution. This includes but is not limited to: Sensitive information; Patient Information; Staff Information; Intellectual Property; Proprietary Code or proprietary information; Passwords; Keys; credit card numbers or other financial information.
- o Only information that is already available in the public domain should be used, unless data access and sharing can be locked down and guaranteed via contractual clauses.
- Trust Login Accounts must not be used for public AI tools such as ChatGPT etc.
- Staff must not use their work (gstt.nhs.uk;rbht.nhs.uk; nhs.net) email address when registering to use an LLM for personal use.
- Don't assume AI security tooling can replace a zero-trust security strategy; Role Based Access Control and Least Privilege must still apply.
- Don't install or use a solution that will require an unauthorised change to Trust systems including desktops, firewall rules, etc.
- Don't install or use a solution that would circumvent Trust policies and standards.
- Don't integrate any AI technology with Trust systems without the correct due diligence and approval.
- DO remember that all Trust policies and standards apply to AI solutions, whether they are proofof-concept (POC) or permanent implementations.
- Remember that an LLM itself may store the information entered into it insecurely or in a country where data protection laws are not in line with UK GDPR, which put GSTT at risk of not being compliant with UK data protection law. Ensure tools comply with all data protection regulations
- Always use LLMs with caution.
- Be aware that LLMs are trained on massive datasets of text and code, are still under development, and they can sometimes generate incorrect or misleading information.
- LLM output must always be verified via human intervention.
- Output from LLMs should be validated and correlated with other trusted sources of information. Fact-check all content.  False positives and negatives do occur.
- DO make sure that user Least Privilege and RBAC are incorporated into the solution.
- Treat the information entered into public AI solutions as if you are posting on a public website.

- Remember that providers can and do monitor conversations to improve their systems and ensure the content complies with their own policies and safety requirements. There are no known assurances regarding their employees, contractors or partners who may view the information you post.  Bear this in mind to prevent a data breach of sensitive information.
- Use Multi-Factor authentication.
- AI prompts should be documented and standardised.
- Ensure that adversarial scenarios are tested against solutions to ensure resilience in the face of manipulative attacks.
- Do ensure when solutions and POCs are retired that all data models are securely deleted along with the data itself, as per Trust retention and trust data destruction standards.  Documentation of these actions must be retained as part of any project.
- When developing AI, make sure that Disaster Recovery and Resilience is considered at solution design stage.

Hallucinations are also sometimes referred to lack of faithfulness or lack of groundedness. In some instances, synthetic data that is generated by large language models might include hallucinations that result in the data possibly being inaccurate, fabricated, or disconnected from reality. Hallucinations can compromise model performance, accuracy, and relevance.
